title: Kalam & Kalima (Speech & Word)
description: Kalam is a complete, meaningful sentence in Arabic. Kalima is a single word. Every Kalima falls into exactly one of three categories: Ism (noun), Fi'l (verb), or Harf (particle). This three-way division is the foundation of all Arabic grammar.

quiz.question: Every word in Arabic must be one of three types. Which of these is NOT one of them?

title: Ism (Noun)
description: An Ism is a word that denotes a person, place, thing, or idea independent of time. It is one of the three fundamental parts of Arabic speech. An Ism can carry grammatical case markers: Raf' (ضمة), Nasb (فتحة), or Jarr (كسرة), and it can accept Tanwin, Al (the definite article), and Idafa.

quiz.question: Which of these is an Ism (noun)?

title: Fi'l (Verb)
description: A Fi'l is a word that denotes an action or state tied to a specific time. There are three types: Maadi (past ماضي), Mudhari' (present/future مضارع), and Amr (command أمر).

quiz.question: Which verb is in the past tense (Maadi)?

title: Harf (Particle)
description: A Harf is a word that has no independent meaning on its own — it only conveys meaning in conjunction with other words. Examples include prepositions, conjunctions, and negation particles. A Harf never takes case endings or Tanwin.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a Harf (particle)?

title: Jumla Ismiyya & Fi'liyya
description: Arabic sentences are of two types. A Jumla Ismiyya (nominal sentence) begins with an Ism and consists of Mubtada + Khabar. A Jumla Fi'liyya (verbal sentence) begins with a Fi'l and consists of Fi'l + Fa'il, emphasizing the occurrence of an action.

quiz.question: A sentence that begins with a verb is called:

title: I'rab — Raf' (Nominative)
description: Raf' is the nominative case, marked by a Damma (ُ) or its equivalent. It is the case of the Subject (Mubtada), Predicate (Khabar), Subject of Kana, Predicate of Inna, and the Doer (Fa'il).

examples.meaning: The book is beautiful — both words are Marfoo' (Raf')
The man came — ar-rajulu is Fa'il (Marfoo')

quiz.question: Which case marker indicates Raf'?

title: I'rab — Nasb (Accusative)
description: Nasb is the accusative/subjunctive case, marked by a Fatha (َ) or its equivalent. It is the case of the direct object (Maf'ul), object of certain particles like إِنَّ, and the Mudhari' Fi'l after Nasb particles (أَنْ، لَنْ، كَيْ).

examples.meaning: I read a book — kitaaban is Maf'ul (Mansub)
I will never lie — akdhiba is Mansub

quiz.question: Which particle causes Nasb on a Mudhari' verb?

title: I'rab — Jarr (Genitive)
description: Jarr is the genitive case, marked by a Kasra (ِ) or its equivalent. A noun takes Jarr when it follows a preposition (Harf Jarr) or is in an Idafa (possessive) construction.

examples.meaning: I went to the mosque — al-masjidi is Majrur
The book of Allah — Allahi is Mudaf ilayh (Majrur)

quiz.question: When does a noun take Jarr?

title: I'rab — Jazm (Jussive)
description: Jazm is a state exclusive to the Mudhari' verb, marked by a Sukun (ْ) or the dropping of the final letter/noon. It occurs after Jazm particles such as لَمْ (did not), لَمَّا (not yet), and in conditional and imperative structures.

examples.meaning: He did not write — yaktub is Majzoom
Do not be afraid — takhaf is Majzoom

quiz.question: Jazm can only occur on which type of word?

title: Mubtada & Khabar
description: A nominal sentence (جملة اسمية) begins with a noun. The subject is called Mubtada (مبتدأ) and is always Marfoo'. The predicate is called Khabar (خبر) and is also Marfoo'. Together they form a complete thought.

examples.meaning: Allah is the Greatest — Allah = Mubtada, Akbar = Khabar

quiz.question: In 'الْكِتَابُ مُفِيدٌ', what is الْكِتَابُ?

title: Fa'il (Doer/Subject)
description: The Fa'il is the doer of the action in a verbal sentence — the one who performs the Fi'l. It always comes after the verb and is always Marfoo'. The verb agrees with the Fa'il in gender but stays singular even if the Fa'il is plural.

examples.meaning: Zayd stood up — Zaydun is Fa'il

quiz.question: What is the grammatical case of the Fa'il?

title: Maf'ul Bihi (Direct Object)
description: The Maf'ul Bihi is the direct object — the noun that receives the action of the verb. It is always in the Nasb (accusative) case and typically follows the Fa'il in a verbal sentence.

examples.meaning: The boy ate the apple — at-tuffaahata is Maf'ul Bihi

quiz.question: What case does the Maf'ul Bihi always take?

title: Na'at (Adjective)
description: Na'at is a descriptive adjective that follows the noun it describes (Man'ut) and must agree with it in four things: case (Raf'/Nasb/Jarr), definiteness, gender, and number.

examples.meaning: A generous man — kareemun describes rajulun

quiz.question: Na'at must agree with the Man'ut in how many things?

title: Ma'rifa & Nakira (Definite & Indefinite)
description: A Nakira (indefinite noun) refers to something unspecific and usually carries Tanwin, like كِتَابٌ (a book). A Ma'rifa (definite noun) refers to something specific — proper names, pronouns, or nouns with الـ (Al), like الْكِتَابُ (the book).

quiz.question: What typically marks a noun as Nakira?

title: Mudhakkar & Mu'annath (Gender)
description: Arabic nouns are either Mudhakkar (masculine) or Mu'annath (feminine). Feminine nouns are usually marked with a Ta Marbuta (ة) at the end, though some feminine words have no visible marker and must be memorised.

quiz.question: Which letter most commonly marks a feminine noun?

title: Mufrad, Muthanna & Jam'
description: Arabic nouns have three numbers: Mufrad (singular — one), Muthanna (dual — exactly two, formed by adding انِ/يْنِ), and Jam' (plural — three or more).

quiz.question: How many things does the Muthanna (dual) refer to?

title: Jam' — Salim & Taksir
description: There are two main plural types: Jam' Salim (sound plural), which keeps the singular form and adds a suffix — ونَ/ينَ for masculine, اتٌ for feminine — and Jam' Taksir (broken plural), where the internal pattern of the word changes irregularly.

quiz.question: What is Jam' Taksir (broken plural)?
options: A plural formed by a regular suffix
A plural with an irregular internal pattern change

title: Dhamir (Pronouns)
description: A Dhamir is a pronoun that stands in place of a noun. Munfasil (detached) pronouns stand alone, like هُوَ (he) and أَنَا (I). Muttasil (attached) pronouns are suffixed to a verb, noun, or particle, like the هُ in كِتَابُهُ (his book).

quiz.question: What is a Dhamir Muttasil?
options: A pronoun attached to another word

title: Ism al-Ishara (Demonstratives)
description: Ism al-Ishara points to something specific. هَذَا (this, masculine), هَذِهِ (this, feminine), ذَلِكَ (that, masculine), and تِلْكَ (that, feminine) are the most common demonstrative pronouns.

quiz.question: Which word means 'this' for a feminine noun?

title: Ism al-Mawsul (Relative Pronouns)
description: Ism al-Mawsul connects a noun to a following descriptive clause (Sila). الَّذِي (who/that, masculine singular) and الَّتِي (who/that, feminine singular) are the most common relative pronouns.

examples.meaning: The one who wrote the lesson came
I saw the one (f) who succeeded

quiz.question: Which relative pronoun is used for a feminine singular?

title: Harf al-Jarr (Prepositions)
description: Prepositions always put the following noun into the Jarr case. Common ones include فِي (in), مِنْ (from), إِلَى (to), عَلَى (on), بِ (with/by), and لِ (for).

quiz.question: What case does a Harf Jarr always require?

title: Fi'l Majhul (Passive Voice)
description: In the passive voice, the doer is unknown or unmentioned, so the direct object takes the position of the subject and is called Na'ib al-Fa'il. The internal vowelling of the verb changes: Damma on the first letter, Kasra before the last.

examples.meaning: The lesson was written — ad-darsu is Na'ib al-Fa'il

quiz.question: In the passive voice, what replaces the Fa'il?

title: Kana & Its Sisters
description: كَانَ and its sisters (كان، أصبح، أمسى، أضحى، صار...) are special verbs that enter on a nominal sentence, put the Mubtada in Raf' (called Ism Kana) and the Khabar in Nasb (called Khabar Kana).

examples.meaning: Allah was/is Ever Forgiving — Allahu=Raf', Ghafooran=Nasb

quiz.question: After كَانَ, what case does the Khabar take?

title: Inna & Its Sisters
description: إِنَّ and its sisters (إن، أن، كأن، لكن، ليت، لعل) enter on a nominal sentence and put the Mubtada in Nasb (Ism Inna) while the Khabar remains in Raf' (Khabar Inna).

examples.meaning: Indeed Allah is Forgiving — Allaha=Nasb, Ghafoor=Raf'

quiz.question: After إِنَّ, what case does the Ism (subject) take?

title: Idafa (Possessive Construction)
description: Idafa is a two-word possessive structure. The first word (Mudaf) never takes Tanwin and is in the case demanded by its position in the sentence. The second word (Mudaf ilayh) is always Majrur (Jarr).

quiz.question: In an Idafa, what case is the Mudaf ilayh always in?

title: Istithna (Exception)
description: Istithna expresses an exception using إِلَّا (except) and similar particles. The excluded noun (Mustathna) usually takes the Nasb case when the sentence is complete and affirmative.

examples.meaning: The students attended except Khalid — Khaalidan is Mansub

quiz.question: Which particle is used to express an exception?

title: Hal (Circumstantial Accusative)
description: Hal is a word, always in the Nasb case, that describes the state or condition of the doer or object at the time of the action. It answers the question 'how?' or 'in what state?'.

examples.meaning: Zayd came riding — raakiban describes his state

quiz.question: What case does the Hal always take?

title: Tamyiz (Specification)
description: Tamyiz is a noun in the Nasb case that clarifies or specifies an ambiguous word before it, often following numbers, weights, measures, or comparisons.

examples.meaning: I have twenty books — kitaaban is Tamyiz

quiz.question: Tamyiz most often follows what kind of word?

title: Nida (Vocative — Calling)
description: Nida is the grammatical structure used to call or address someone, using particles like يَا. The noun being called (Munada) is typically Marfoo' if it is a single definite name.

quiz.question: Which particle is most commonly used for calling someone?

title: Adawat al-Shart (Conditional Particles)
description: Conditional particles like إِنْ (if) and مَنْ (whoever) introduce a condition clause (Fi'l ash-Shart) followed by a result clause (Jawab ash-Shart). Both verbs are typically in Jazm.

examples.meaning: If you strive, you will succeed

quiz.question: What is the mood of the verbs in a conditional sentence with إِنْ?

title: Arabic Root System
description: Almost all Arabic words are derived from a 3-letter root (sometimes 4-letter). Understanding the root unlocks the meaning of hundreds of related words. The root carries the core semantic meaning, while patterns (Awzan أوزان) determine the exact word form.

examples.meaning: Root of all words related to writing
He wrote, book, writer, office, written

quiz.question: What is the root of كِتَابٌ (book)?

title: Wazn — The Pattern System
description: Arabic morphology uses a pattern system (Awzan) to derive words. The root letters are substituted into patterns built on ف-ع-ل. For example, فَاعِل is the pattern for 'doer', giving كَاتِب (writer) from ك-ت-ب.

quiz.question: What is the Wazn (pattern) of كَاتِب (writer)?

title: Thulathi Mujarrad (Bare Triliteral)
description: Thulathi Mujarrad is the simplest verb form, consisting of exactly three root letters with no extra letters added, such as فَعَلَ (fa'ala). It is the base from which all augmented forms are derived.

examples.meaning: He helped — 3 root letters, no addition

quiz.question: How many letters does a Thulathi Mujarrad verb have?

title: Thulathi Mazid (Augmented Triliteral)
description: Thulathi Mazid verbs add one, two, or three extra letters to the bare triliteral root to create new but related meanings — such as intensity, causation, or reciprocity. These form the famous 'ten forms' (Awzan) of Arabic verbs.

quiz.question: What does Thulathi Mazid mean?
options: A verb with no extra letters
A verb with extra letters added to the root

title: Form II — Fa''ala (تفعيل)
description: Form II doubles the middle root letter and often conveys intensity or causation (making someone do the action). Its Masdar pattern is typically تَفْعِيل.

examples.meaning: He taught (caused to know) — from عَلِمَ (he knew)
He smashed to pieces (intensive) — from كَسَرَ (he broke)

quiz.question: What is the defining feature of Form II verbs?

title: Form III — Faa'ala (مفاعلة)
description: Form III adds an Alif after the first root letter and typically expresses an action done towards or with another person (reciprocity or effort directed at someone).

examples.meaning: He fought (with someone) — from قَتَلَ (he killed)

quiz.question: What does Form III (فَاعَلَ) typically express?

title: Form IV — Af'ala (إفعال)
description: Form IV prefixes a Hamza to the root and usually conveys causation — making someone else do or become something. Its Masdar pattern is إِفْعَال.

examples.meaning: He honoured (made generous to) — from كَرُمَ (he was noble)
He believed — from أَمِنَ (he was safe)

quiz.question: What prefix defines Form IV verbs?

title: Form V — Tafa''ala (تفعُّل)
description: Form V adds تَ before Form II's pattern and often expresses the reflexive of Form II — doing the action to oneself, or gradually undergoing a process.

examples.meaning: He learned (taught himself) — from عَلَّمَ (he taught)

quiz.question: Form V is typically the reflexive of which form?

title: Form VI — Tafaa'ala (تفاعُل)
description: Form VI adds تَ before Form III's pattern, expressing mutual or reciprocal action performed between two or more parties together.

quiz.question: What does Form VI typically express?

title: Form VII — Infa'ala (انفعال)
description: Form VII prefixes اِنْـ to the root and almost always conveys a passive or reflexive meaning — something happening to the subject without an active agent expressed.

examples.meaning: It broke / got broken — from كَسَرَ (he broke it)

quiz.question: Form VII (اِنْفَعَلَ) typically conveys:

title: Form VIII — Ifta'ala (افتعال)
description: Form VIII infixes تَ after the first root letter, often conveying reflexive action, effort, or a meaning close to the root but affecting the subject itself.

quiz.question: Where is the extra ت placed in Form VIII?
options: Infixed after the first root letter

title: Form X — Istaf'ala (استفعال)
description: Form X prefixes اِسْتَـ to the root and typically expresses seeking, requesting, or considering something to have a quality — 'to seek/ask for X'.

examples.meaning: He sought forgiveness — from غَفَرَ (He forgave)

quiz.question: What does Form X (اِسْتَفْعَلَ) typically express?

title: Verb Conjugation — Maadi (Past Tense)
description: The past tense verb (Maadi) is the base form in Arabic. It is conjugated for person (1st, 2nd, 3rd), gender (masculine/feminine), and number (singular, dual, plural) using suffixes.

quiz.question: What suffix do you add to a past tense verb for 'I' (1st person singular)?

title: Verb Conjugation — Mudhari' (Present/Future)
description: The Mudhari' tense expresses present or future actions. It is formed by adding prefixes (و ن ت أ — wanataa) and sometimes suffixes to the root. It is always Marfoo' by default unless a Nasb or Jazm particle precedes it.

quiz.question: Which prefix is used for 3rd person masculine singular Mudhari'?

title: Fi'l al-Amr (Imperative)
description: Fi'l al-Amr is the command form, derived from the Mudhari' by dropping the present-tense prefix and adjusting the ending. It is only used for the 2nd person (you) and always ends in Sukun, dropped noon, or a stable letter.

quiz.question: Fi'l al-Amr is used to address which grammatical person?

title: Active & Passive Participles
description: Ism al-Fa'il (اسم الفاعل) is the active participle — 'the one who does'. Its pattern is فَاعِل. Ism al-Maf'ul (اسم المفعول) is the passive participle — 'the one who is acted upon'. Its pattern is مَفْعُول.

quiz.question: What is the pattern for Ism al-Fa'il (active participle)?

title: Masdar — The Verbal Noun
description: The Masdar is the verbal noun — it expresses the action without reference to time, doer, or gender. For Form I verbs, the Masdar is irregular and must be memorised. For Forms II–X, the Masdar follows fixed patterns.

quiz.question: What is the Masdar (verbal noun) of سَبَّحَ (Form II)?

title: Ism Tafdil (Comparative/Superlative)
description: Ism Tafdil expresses 'more/most' comparisons, formed mainly on the pattern أَفْعَل from a Thulathi Mujarrad root. It is used both comparatively (bigger than) and superlatively (the biggest).

examples.meaning: He is better than his brother

quiz.question: What is the typical pattern of Ism Tafdil?

title: Ism al-Makan wal-Zaman
description: Ism Makan (noun of place) and Ism Zaman (noun of time) indicate where or when an action takes place. From Thulathi Mujarrad they commonly follow the pattern مَفْعَل or مَفْعِل.

examples.meaning: Office / place of writing — from ك ت ب
Place/time of sunset — from غ ر ب

quiz.question: Ism Makan wal-Zaman indicates:
options: The place or time of an action

title: Ism al-Aala (Noun of Instrument)
description: Ism al-Aala names the tool or instrument used to perform an action. Common patterns include مِفْعَل, مِفْعَلَة, and مِفْعَال.

examples.meaning: Key (instrument for opening) — from ف ت ح

quiz.question: Ism al-Aala refers to:

title: Sahih & Mu'tal Verbs
description: A Fi'l Sahih has three sound root letters with no و، ا، or ي among them, and conjugates regularly. A Fi'l Mu'tal contains one of these weak letters, causing irregular changes during conjugation.

examples.meaning: He wrote — Sahih (sound, no weak letters)
He said / He called / He threw — all Mu'tal (contain weak letters)

quiz.question: What makes a verb Mu'tal (weak)?
options: It contains و، ا، or ي in its root

title: Tathniya (Dual Formation)
description: To form the Muthanna (dual) of a noun, add انِ in the Raf' case or يْنِ in the Nasb/Jarr cases to the singular, after removing Tanwin.

quiz.question: Which suffix marks the dual in the Nasb/Jarr case?

title: Jam' Mudhakkar & Mu'annath Salim
description: Jam' Mudhakkar Salim (sound masculine plural) adds ونَ (Raf') or ينَ (Nasb/Jarr) to the singular. Jam' Mu'annath Salim (sound feminine plural) adds اتٌ to the singular, most often for words ending in Ta Marbuta.

quiz.question: What suffix forms the sound feminine plural?

title: Al-Muzari' — Signs of I'rab
description: The Mudhari' verb shows its case through changing endings: Damma for Raf', Fatha for Nasb, and Sukun (or dropped noon in the five verbs) for Jazm — unlike the Maadi, which never changes for case.

examples.meaning: He will never write — Fatha ending
He did not write — Sukun ending

quiz.question: Which verb type can show Raf', Nasb, and Jazm case endings?
